name: Dinka
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Malou, Job. 1988. Dinka Vowel System. SIL Publications in Linguistics 82. Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics & University of Texas at Arlington. (ERIC ED 297 580 microfiche scan, archive.org)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.2 'The Phonological Word', p. 9 (example (5) p. 10); sec. 2 preamble p. 8; sec. 2.3 p. 10; ch. 5 'Tone' p. 61.
catalog_quote: Described in terms of the elements distributed in it and the features which characterize it, the phonological word is the unit of stress placement in the phonological hierarchy. Each phonological word has one and only one stress. The factors that condition stress have not been studied and, as mentioned, are not the concern of this discussion. It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis in Dinka. The final margin of the phonological word is characterized by potential pause. The phonological word is the level of distribution of the syllable: one syllable is stressed in each word.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka is a tone language (with contrastive three-level vowel length and voice quality) whose words are overwhelmingly monosyllabic. Malou says every phonological word carries exactly one non-contrastive stress but that what determines which syllable carries it 'has not been studied'; no placement rule is given. Later work is either silent (Blum 2023, van Urk 2015, Mayom 2014 on Bor) or sceptical: van Urk & Chong (2025 ms) say Dinka 'lacks an obvious stress system' (root-final syllable is the prominent/morphology-bearing position), and Remijsen & Manyang 2009 report that Remijsen & Gilley 2008 found no acoustic support for Gilley's (2003) stress in the Rek dialect Luanyjang.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Malou explicitly leaves the conditioning of stress unstudied. Malou's example (5) marks stress on words in short phrases without stating a rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (defined as the domain bounded by potential pause); statement is for Dinka as a whole (pan-dialectal), not specifically Bor; Malou's phonological sketch also describes sentence-level intonation (declarative downdrift etc.) separately (sec. 2.1).
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand stress statement found (Malou 1988) is a pan-Dinka description covering all four major varieties (Eastern = Bor based, Northern/Padang, Southern/Agar, Western/Rek; Malou p. 1); the author is a native speaker whose own variety is not stated in the pages read (the earlier scan note calls him a Bor-area speaker; his acoustic-study speakers are labelled 'southern' and 'eastern', eastern = Bor-based in his classification). Every Bor-specific source opened (Blum 2023 on Bor South, van Urk 2015 on Bor, Mayom 2014 on Bor, Remijsen 2013 on Bor South/North) is silent on word stress. The sceptical statements (Remijsen & Manyang 2009 fn. 5; van Urk & Chong 2025 ms 'Dinka lacks an obvious stress system') concern Luanyjang/Rek (sout2832) and Agar (dib, sout.. South Central) respectively, extended by the authors to Dinka generally. Sister-glottocode check sout2832 (Southwestern Dinka) already holds the Malou file and reaches the same statement.

new_statements.quote: [p.5] The stress mark found in example (1) means that the vowel is about half the length of the unstressed counterpart in example (2). Both vowels have Low tone. ... Low tone plus stress indicates 2ps Agent while Low tone without stress indicates 3ps Agent ... [p.10] However, in my analysis, that length is the result of one of the words being stressed while the other is unstressed. Stressed words in Dinka shorten the vowel to about half its original length. Thus, the shorter of the vowels is said to be stressed. ... The term “stress” has been used to distinguish the length variations between extra short and short and between short and long.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog classification tonal (two level tones plus HF, LF, Rise contours, p.11). Differs from the Malou 1988 statement held by the project ('stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis'; one stress per phonological word, conditioning unstudied): Gilley asserts that 'not only tone, but also stress is very important for indicating grammatical information' (p.3) and that Dinka orthography must mark 'tonal and stress contrasts' (p.12), with stressed/unstressed minimal pairs on CVC roots (pp.5, 10). The difference is largely one of construct: Gilley's 'stress' is by her own statement (p.10) a relabelling of the vowel-length grades (Andersen'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka is tonal (p.11: 'Dinka has two level tones and the contour tones High fall, Low fall, and Rise'). Gilley uses 'stress' for a word-level feature of the (mostly monosyllabic CVC) root that carries grammatical contrasts: stressed vs unstressed distinguishes 2sg vs 3sg readers on verbs (exx. 1-2, 47-48), readers-first vs object-focus clauses (4-5, 50-51) and singular vs plural nouns (41-43); phonetically a stressed word has its vowel shortened to about half. She states explicitly that 'stress' is her label for Andersen's (1993) length grades (extra-short vs short, short vs long), i.e. a reanalysis of three-degree vowel length as two lengths plus stress, and proposes writing the unstressed word with a final apostrophe. Nothing is said about where stress falls within polysyllabic words; no placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Underlyingly short-vowel roots cannot lengthen: singular 'extra short' vs plural 'just short' or 'lowered' (diphthongised, Duerksen 1989 term), ex. (43) p.10; the Dinka themselves reject a three-way length distinction and 'see it as a two-way distinction only' (p.10).
new_statements.identity_note: Gilley's Dinka examples are Rek dialect, stated (p.4) to be representative of Rek, Bor, Agaar and Padang; conclusion mentions work with four Dinka dialects. The catalog's Malou 1988 statement is pan-Dinka. sout2834 is the Glottolog Dinka macro-node used by the catalog entry 'Dinka'.

tone_statements.citation: Blum, Mirella L. 2025. Dialectal tone description enhances historical tonology. Diachronica 42(3-4): 305-323. doi:10.1075/dia.24021.blu
tone_statements.quote: All described dialects of Dinka have either three or four tones: Low (L, v̀); High (H, v́); Fall (HL, v̂); and, in four-toned dialects, Rise (LH, v̌) (Andersen 1987; Remijsen & Ladd 2008; Remijsen 2010; Blum 2020, 2023). The tone-bearing unit of Dinka is the syllable. … The contour tones in question – HL and LH – are analyzed as compositional due to their behavior in contextual tonal processes … Bor South has four tones as well, but exhibits non-final neutralization of the High and Fall tones; it would be placed in Stage 2A.

tone_statements.summary: Bor South Dinka: four tones Low, High, Fall (HL), Rise (LH) on the syllable, contours built from two heights; Fall surfaces as High non-finally; Bor South generally lacks Aliap's automatic downstep.

tone_statements.quote: In addition, Dinka is tonal; all dialects for which descriptions exist have either three or four tonemes. The Bor South dialect has four tones: Low (L, v̀); High (H, v́); Fall (HL, v̂); and Rise (LH, v̌) (Remijsen 2013). Finally, Dinka is largely monosyllabic, with the following syllable structure: C(w/j)V(V)(V)C, where parentheses represent optional syllabic elements. … voice quality and tone are indicated on the first vowel symbol, as is the convention in recent literature on Dinka.
tone_statements.summary: Bor South Dinka has four tonemes: Low, High, Fall, Rise (after Remijsen 2013); other dialects have three or four. Adjectival verbs have a Low-toned finite form; negation raises verb tone to High.

readall_conflicts: Gilley 2004 agrees with the catalog that Dinka is a tone language (two level tones plus High-fall, Low-fall and Rise contours, p.11) and, like Malou 1988, gives no rule for where stress falls. It disagrees at face value with the Malou 1988 statement held by the project that stress is 'neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis': Gilley treats 'stress' as a grammatically contrastive feature of the CVC root (stressed vs unstressed word = 2sg vs 3sg readers, readers-first vs object-focus verb forms, singular vs plural nouns; pp.5, 10, 12). By her own statement (p.10) this 'stress' is a relabelling of the vowel-length grades that Andersen (1993) analyses as three degrees of length (stressed = vowel shortened to about half), so the conflict is about the construct called stress rather than about stress placement; the catalog entry (tonal, no placement rule) stands, with the note that 'stress' in the SIL/Gilley Dinka literature means the short length grade.

sources.citation: Blum, Mirella L. 2020. Cross-dialect Variation in Dinka Tonal Morphology. MSc dissertation, University of Edinburgh. 41 pp.
sources.note: Describes the tone system of the previously undocumented Hol dialect and compares it with Bor South (both Bor cluster = Southeastern Dinka). Hol has four tonemes, Low, High, Fall (HL) and Rise (LH), the syllable is the TBU, with allotonic realizations by context and a Low Absorption neutralization; Bor South has the same four tonemes with utterance-medial neutralization of Fall with High (sec. 3.3-3.4, pp. 21-28). Second part: a tonal change on transitive verbs (first noted for Agar) is shown to be a separate inflectional category in Hol and Bor South (tonal morphology).
